input.strategy_title: Make RHOAI more usable for enterprise teams
input.strategy_markdown:
## Problem Statement

Several strategic accounts have told field teams that RHOAI "feels hard to use
at enterprise scale". Feedback arrived through different channels and has not
been consolidated; the quotes below are representative but partially
contradictory. Leadership wants visible usability progress this release.

## High-Level Requirements

| ID | Priority | Requirement |
|-------|----------|-------------|
| HLR-1 | — | Administration should be simpler. One account wants fewer configuration options exposed ("too many knobs"), another explicitly wants more fine-grained controls per project. |
| HLR-2 | — | Onboarding a new data scientist should take "less than a day". It is not defined what onboarding includes or where the day is currently spent. |
| HLR-3 | — | The platform should "integrate better" with existing enterprise tooling. No specific tools were named in the consolidated feedback. |
| HLR-4 | P2 | Publish a whitepaper describing enterprise usability best practices on RHOAI. |

## Affected Components

- Dashboard
- Notebooks

## Out of Scope

Nothing has been explicitly scoped out.

## Open Questions

1. Which accounts' feedback takes precedence when requirements conflict (HLR-1)?
2. What does "onboarding" cover for HLR-2 — cluster access, project setup,
   first workbench, or first deployed model?
3. Which enterprise tools does HLR-3 actually mean?

# Resolve the conflicting enterprise requirements for admin configuration

## Description

This investigation resolves the contradiction inside the strategy's
administration requirement: one strategic account wants fewer configuration
options exposed ("too many knobs") while another explicitly wants more
fine-grained per-project controls. The enterprise feedback behind both asks is
scattered across field channels and has never been consolidated. This epic
consolidates that feedback, characterizes the conflict, and drives a recorded
decision on which direction (simplification, fine-grained controls, or a
hybrid such as progressive disclosure) the platform will pursue — the decision
that determines what the admin-configuration implementation builds.

## Scope

- Gather the enterprise-account feedback about administration complexity from
  all field channels (account teams, support escalations, filed quotes).
- Produce a consolidated feedback inventory: per account, what was asked, in
  what terms, through which channel.
- Characterize the HLR-1 conflict: which accounts want simplification, which
  want more control, and what each is actually trying to accomplish.
- Draft resolution options (reduce exposed configuration, add per-project
  fine-grained controls, or a hybrid that hides complexity behind sensible
  defaults while keeping advanced control reachable), with the user value and
  cost of each.
- Drive the precedence decision with product management and the account teams
  — including which accounts' feedback takes precedence when requirements
  conflict — and record the outcome and rationale in a decision record.

## Acceptance Criteria

- A consolidated feedback inventory exists that lists each contributing
  account's administration-related ask and its source channel; no known
  feedback channel is omitted.
- A decision record states which direction is pursued (simplification,
  fine-grained per-project controls, or a named hybrid) and why, including the
  precedence rule applied between conflicting accounts.
- Both sides of the conflict are explicitly addressed: the decision record
  states how the losing concern is handled (satisfied by the chosen design,
  deferred with rationale, or declined with rationale).
- An implementer reading only the decision record can determine what to build
  — no further account arbitration is required to start implementation.

## HLR Traceability

- **HLR-1** (Administration should be simpler; conflicting account feedback on
  configuration exposure) — this epic resolves the requirement's internal
  conflict so it can be implemented at all.

# Define data-scientist onboarding scope and locate where the onboarding day is spent

## Description

The strategy requires that onboarding a new data scientist take "less than a
day", but neither what onboarding covers nor where the day is currently spent
is defined. This investigation defines the onboarding scope (which of cluster
access, project setup, first workbench, first deployed model — or other stages
discovered during the study — are in bounds) and produces a time breakdown of
the current journey, so the onboarding-improvement work targets the actual
cost centers instead of a guess.

## Scope

- Enumerate the candidate onboarding stages from account access to first
  productive work (cluster access, project setup, first workbench, first
  deployed model, plus any additional stages the study surfaces).
- Define which stages the "less than a day" target covers, with an explicit
  boundary and rationale, and get that definition accepted by product
  management.
- Measure or estimate current elapsed time per stage, using available
  evidence: deployment telemetry, support tickets, field/account reports, and
  direct observation of representative new-user sessions.
- Produce a ranked list of time cost centers identifying where the day is
  actually lost.
- Recommend which stage(s) the onboarding-time reduction work should target,
  with expected time savings per stage.

## Acceptance Criteria

- An onboarding definition exists that states the included stages and the
  explicit out-of-bounds boundary, accepted by product management.
- A per-stage time breakdown exists, with the evidence source cited for each
  stage's figure.
- A ranked cost-center list identifies the dominant time consumers in the
  defined onboarding scope.
- A recommendation names the stage(s) to target for the under-a-day goal and
  estimates the time recoverable from each.

## HLR Traceability

- **HLR-2** (Onboarding a new data scientist should take less than a day; it
  is not defined what onboarding includes or where the day is currently spent)
  — this epic supplies the missing definition and diagnosis that the
  implementation depends on.

# Identify the enterprise tools meant by the integration feedback

## Description

The strategy requires the platform to "integrate better" with existing
enterprise tooling, but the consolidated feedback names no specific tools.
This investigation determines which tools the feedback actually refers to and
produces a prioritized integration target list with an integration-surface
hypothesis per tool, so the integration work builds against named targets
instead of an unspecified "better integration".

## Scope

- Consolidate the tool-related enterprise feedback from all field channels
  (account teams, support, filed quotes), coordinating with the parallel
  feedback-consolidation effort for the admin-configuration question rather
  than duplicating it.
- Interview the account and field teams to attach concrete tool names to the
  vague "integrate better" asks.
- For each candidate tool, record the source feedback, the integration
  surface where RHOAI would plausibly connect (as visible from the
  platform's architecture context), and a rough feasibility and impact
  assessment.
- Produce a prioritized shortlist of integration targets with rationale,
  reviewed by product management.

## Acceptance Criteria

- Every candidate tool is named with the feedback or interview that motivated
  it — no tool enters the list without a traceable source.
- A prioritized shortlist exists with, per tool, the rationale, a feasibility
  note, and an integration-surface hypothesis.
- The shortlist has been reviewed and its ordering accepted by product
  management.
- If the investigation concludes that no concrete tool set can be identified
  from the available feedback, that conclusion is recorded with the evidence
  gap stated, so the requirement can be returned to refinement.

## HLR Traceability

- **HLR-3** (The platform should integrate better with existing enterprise
  tooling; no specific tools were named in the consolidated feedback) — this
  epic converts the unnamed requirement into named, prioritized targets.

# Deliver the resolved admin-configuration experience

## Description

This epic implements the admin-configuration direction chosen by the
enterprise-feedback consolidation and precedence decision — reducing exposed
configuration complexity, adding fine-grained per-project controls, or the
hybrid the decision record specifies. The Dashboard is the surface where
per-component feature flags and defaults are administered, so the
implementation lands in its configuration and settings surfaces. The scope
below is deliberately at the functional level of the strategy; the decision
record fixes the direction and the implementing team fixes the design.

## Scope

- Implement the chosen admin-configuration direction in the Dashboard's
  configuration surfaces, exactly as specified by the decision record from
  the feedback-consolidation investigation (sensible defaults with reduced
  exposed options, per-project fine-grained controls, or the specified
  hybrid).
- Address or explicitly carry forward the deferred concerns recorded in the
  decision record for the accounts on the losing side of the conflict.
- Cover the incidental documentation touch-ups that fall out of the change
  (updated captions, references, and screenshots for the changed surfaces) —
  no separate content effort.

## Acceptance Criteria

- The admin-configuration experience matches the decision record: an
  implementer-independent review can verify each decision-record item is
  delivered or tracked as deferred.
- Changes to the existing configuration exposure ship with a rollback path
  (feature flag or equivalent), since this work replaces or restructures
  capability that strategic accounts currently use.
- The concerns of both conflicting accounts are demonstrably handled: each is
  either satisfied by the delivered design or covered by the recorded
  deferral/decline rationale.
- The Dashboard's existing build and test pipeline is green on the delivered
  change.

## HLR Traceability

- **HLR-1** (Administration should be simpler — resolving the conflict
  between "fewer knobs" and "more fine-grained controls per project") — this
  epic delivers the requirement once its direction is decided.

# Cut new-data-scientist onboarding time to under a day

## Description

This epic implements the onboarding-time reduction for new data scientists so
that the onboarding journey, as defined by the onboarding scope-and-time
study, completes in under a day. The expected target is the workbench
experience — the notebook-server lifecycle from spawn to first productive
use, including startup, image availability, and idle behavior — but the
stages actually attacked are the dominant cost centers identified by that
study. If the study locates the time cost primarily outside the workbench
experience, this epic's scope is rewritten (or re-assigned to the owning
component) per its gate outcome.

## Scope

- Implement improvements to the stage(s) the onboarding study identified as
  the dominant time cost centers, within the workbench experience (workbench
  spawn and startup, image pulling and availability, first-use
  configuration).
- Meet the "under a day" target for the onboarding scope as defined and
  accepted in that study.
- Include any incidental documentation touch-ups for changed behavior (no
  new standalone content).

## Acceptance Criteria

- A run-through of the defined onboarding scope by a representative new data
  scientist (or a validated measurement equivalent) completes in under a day.
- Each implemented improvement maps to a cost center named in the onboarding
  study's ranked list — no speculative improvements outside the identified
  cost centers.
- Changed workbench behavior is covered by regression tests.
- The workbench components' existing build and test pipeline is green on the
  delivered change.

## HLR Traceability

- **HLR-2** (Onboarding a new data scientist should take less than a day) —
  this epic delivers the time reduction once the scope and cost centers are
  known.

# Integrate RHOAI with the identified enterprise tools

## Description

This epic implements the enterprise-tool integrations for the tools named and
prioritized by the tool-identification investigation. Until that list exists
there is nothing concrete to integrate, so this work is gated on it. The
integrations surface through the platform's user-facing console and its
Kubernetes interfaces; the specific integration mechanics per tool follow the
integration-surface hypotheses recorded in that investigation's shortlist.

## Scope

- Implement integrations for the prioritized tools on the accepted shortlist,
  following each tool's recorded integration-surface hypothesis.
- Validate each integration against the real enterprise tool where one is
  available in a test environment, or against a documented representative
  stand-in where it is not.
- Include the incidental documentation touch-ups that fall out of the
  integrations (references and captions only — no new standalone content).

## Acceptance Criteria

- Every integration delivered corresponds to a tool on the accepted
  shortlist; no unlisted tool is integrated.
- Each integration demonstrably works against the real tool or its documented
  representative stand-in, with the validation method recorded.
- Integration failures and limitations discovered during validation are
  documented and triaged.
- The owning components' existing build and test pipeline is green on the
  delivered change.

## HLR Traceability

- **HLR-3** (The platform should integrate better with existing enterprise
  tooling) — this epic delivers the integrations once the target tools are
  identified.

# Publish the enterprise usability best-practices whitepaper

## Description

This epic authors and publishes the whitepaper describing enterprise
usability best practices on RHOAI, as required by the strategy. The
whitepaper consolidates what the usability workstream learned and delivered —
the resolved admin-configuration guidance, the onboarding practices that got
a new data scientist productive in under a day, and the enterprise-tool
integration patterns — into externally usable best-practice guidance. It is
authored through the Red Hat docs content process and therefore runs last,
after the implementations it describes have landed.

## Scope

Content outline (topics to be authored inside this epic):

- **Enterprise administration practices** — how to expose and govern RHOAI
  configuration for enterprise teams, reflecting the resolved
  admin-configuration direction.
- **Data-scientist onboarding practices** — the defined onboarding scope and
  the practices that achieve the under-a-day target.
- **Enterprise tool integration patterns** — how RHOAI connects to the
  identified enterprise tools and how to configure the integrations.
- **Measurement guidance** — how enterprise teams can measure their own
  onboarding and administration friction against the baselines established
  by the usability investigations.

Additional scope:

- Draft, technical review, and publication through the Red Hat docs content
  process.
- Validate all technical claims against the platform's architecture context
  and the delivered implementations.

## Acceptance Criteria

- The whitepaper covers every topic in the content outline above.
- Every technical claim is technically reviewed against the implemented
  capabilities and the platform's architecture context, with review sign-off
  recorded.
